catalog_quote: [p.294] The dialects associated with Orokolo - Muru, Aheave, Belepa, Keuru and Opao - all show a close affinity with it, much more so than the affinity between the forms of speech that make up the Eastern group. All the Western Eleman forms of speech are characterised by the absence of the phonemes /f/ and /s/, which are present elsewhere. [p.307, sec. 8.15.1 Toaripi Phonology] Stress: Words of two or three syllables usually take the stress on the penultimate syllable, e.g. haro /háro/ head, sosoru /sosóru/ firefly. There are some exceptions; e.g. faitora /faitorá/ now. Final diphthongs take the stress as though two syllables, e.g. mapai /mapái/ hear. ... Where there are four or more syllables, there is a minor stress on the syllable two removed from the main penultimate stress; thus karikara /kàrikára/ village. new_statements.rule_in_words: Main stress on the penultimate syllable of the word (stated first-hand for Toaripi and declared identical for Orokolo, the Western Eleman language with which Opao is grouped as an associated dialect); final diphthongs count as two syllables; nominative personal pronouns (ara 'I', are 'he', ela 'we excl.', ere 'they') are finally stressed, reverting to penultimate when the object marker -ro or genitive ve is added; in words of four or more syllables a minor stress falls two syllables before the main stress; reduplications repeat the stem stress; onomatopoeic words often reverse the pattern.
new_statements.secondary_stress: In words of four or more syllables a minor stress on the syllable two removed from the main penultimate stress (karikara /kàrikára/); compounds follow the same pattern; reduplicated words repeat the stress of the stem (Brown 1973:307; 1986:xiv).
new_statements.exceptions: Nominative personal pronouns ara, are, ela, ere with final stress (distinguishing them from penult-stressed homographs, e.g. are 'new'); lexical exceptions such as faitora 'now', pitoo 'swamp crayfish' with final stress; havou 'game' (explained as loss of /h/ from havohu); onomatopoeic words (kekekeke, hohohoho) with reversed pattern.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement for citation forms; Brown separately describes close juncture within the noun phrase where demonstrative+noun, noun+adjective, noun+postposition form one phonological word with the main stress shifting to the adjective/postposition (1973:307-308), and phrase intonation with the accent 'mostly on the last major stressed syllable in the phrase' (p.309). CAVEAT: the statement is made for Toaripi and extended by the author to Orokolo (1973:350; 1986:xiv 'In both Orokolo and Toaripi.. the stress is normally on the penultimate syllable'); Opao itself has no phonology section and is covered only by Brown's grouping of Opao among 'the dialects associated with Orokolo' (p.294) within Western Eleman (Table 3, p.295).
new_statements.identity_note: No source describes Opao (opao1240) phonology by name. The quoted stress rule is Brown's first-hand description of Toaripi (toar1246, Eastern Eleman), which he states holds identically for Orokolo (orok1267, Western Eleman) in 1973:350 and 1986:xiv. Opao is reached only through Brown's classification of Opao as one of 'the dialects associated with Orokolo' (1973:294; Table 3 p.295, Western Eleman Linguistic Group, pop. 1,116 in 1973). Glottolog treats Opao as a separate language (nucl1580 > west2573 > opao1240), sister to Orokolo and Keoru-Ahia. Any catalog entry would therefore be an inference from the Orokolo/Toaripi statement, not an Opao description; hence not proposed for the catalog despite the first-hand quote being held by the project.
